paragraphs: Apprenticeship learning asks how an agent can learn useful behavior by watching an expert when the reward for its actions is unknown. This paper assumes that the true reward is a linear combination of known, observable features. That assumption gives the learner a structured family of possible rewards to work with.

The authors frame the learning problem as a game and apply a multiplicative-weights algorithm for repeated matrix games. Given enough examples, their method is guaranteed to learn a policy nearly as good as the expert’s. It may also produce a substantially better policy, although improvement beyond the expert is a possibility rather than the guarantee.

Compared with the earlier approach discussed in the abstract, the algorithm is faster computationally and easier to implement. The authors also describe applicability without an expert, sketch an extension for unknown environment transitions, and demonstrate the method in a toy video game. The contribution connects a formal performance guarantee with a simpler computational approach to learning behavior.
neurips-2007-a-game-theoretic-approach-t.tldr: A game-theoretic apprenticeship algorithm can learn near-expert behavior under a structured reward assumption and may outperform its teacher.

paragraphs: A numerical measure of dependence does not by itself establish whether an observed relationship is statistically significant. This paper addresses that distinction for the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, or HSIC, a kernel-based measure used in machine learning. The authors turn this measure into a statistical test of the hypothesis that two variables are independent.

The resulting test has computational cost quadratic in the sample size: increasing the number of observations increases the work according to O(m²). Its contribution is therefore both statistical and computational. It supplies a way to assess evidence against independence while stating how the cost of that assessment grows with the available data.

The reported demonstrations show better performance than established tests based on contingency tables and functional correlation, with a larger advantage for multivariate data. The authors also show applicability to text and more general structured data. This broadens the kinds of observations for which the proposed procedure can assess dependence, beyond settings naturally represented by simple numerical variables.
neurips-2007-a-kernel-statistical-test-o.tldr: The paper turns HSIC into a quadratic-cost statistical independence test that also applies to text and structured data.

paragraphs: Generating a talking face requires a model of how facial movements correspond to speech. This paper treats the face and the sound as separate modeling problems, connected through phonemes, the speech units used to link them. This organization gives the animation system an intermediate description of speech from which it can generate movement.

The proposed model is sequential: it generates facial animation from an ordered sequence of phonemes obtained from speech. The central task is therefore to produce a sequence of facial movements corresponding to that speech sequence. The authors evaluate whether this probabilistic approach provides a suitable basis for realistic animation.

Evaluation combines two kinds of evidence. The authors measure differences between generated sequences and real video, and they conduct a double-blind study with human participants. Their experiments report favorable comparisons with existing methods and generated sequences comparable to real video. Together, these assessments support the approach through both measured agreement and human evaluation, without establishing that every generated sequence is indistinguishable from a recording.
neurips-2007-a-probabilistic-model-for-g.tldr: A sequential probabilistic model uses phonemes to connect speech with facial animation, producing favorable measured and human evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies a learning objective called Maximal Average Margin, or MAM. The objective uses the average margin as an optimality principle for designing learning algorithms. Applying it produces computationally simple learning machines resembling the classical Parzen window classifier, connecting a margin-based design principle with an established form of classification.

The authors establish a direct relationship between this principle and Rademacher complexities, mathematical quantities used to analyze learning methods. That relationship supports theoretical analysis and provides a notion of certainty for predictions. They also connect the analysis to support vector machines through a transformation of the margin, relating the proposed approach to another margin-based learning framework.

The paper further applies MAM to ordinal regression, where the prediction task concerns ordered outcomes. This produces an O(n) algorithm, giving linear computational scaling in n and allowing large datasets to be processed in reasonable time. The broader contribution is a design principle that yields simple algorithms while retaining connections to learning theory and prediction certainty.
neurips-2007-a-risk-minimization-princip.tldr: Maximizing average margin yields simple Parzen-like learning methods, theoretical measures of prediction certainty, and a linear-time ordinal regression algorithm.

paragraphs: Music recommendation systems can use listener-supplied tags to organize songs around activities or moods. But tracks with few or no tags are difficult to place within that system. This paper proposes predicting social tags directly from MP3 audio, giving otherwise poorly described music an entry point into a tag-based recommender.

The method uses boosted classifiers to map audio features to tags gathered from the Web. Its output is a set of automatic tags, or autotags, describing a track in the vocabulary already used by the social recommendation system. The connection between sound and user-created descriptions lets the system supply tag information before listeners have provided it.

The authors describe two uses for these predictions. Autotags allow previously unheard music to enter the recommender, addressing the cold-start problem caused by missing tags. They can also provide comparable baseline descriptions across all tracks, smoothing the tag space used to compute similarities and recommendations. This second use concerns consistency across the catalog, including music that already has some human annotations.
neurips-2007-automatic-generation-of-soc.tldr: Boosted classifiers predict social music tags from audio to introduce untagged songs into recommenders and provide consistent catalog descriptions.

paragraphs: Co-training uses multiple views of data in a learning setting that includes unlabeled examples. This paper introduces a Bayesian undirected graphical model for that setting. The model makes explicit assumptions that had remained implicit in a broad class of co-training algorithms and clarifies circumstances in which those assumptions break down.

The authors use insights from this formulation to develop a new co-training kernel for Gaussian process classifiers. They describe the resulting approach as convex, avoiding the local-maxima problems encountered by some earlier multi-view methods. Thus, the probabilistic formulation contributes both an explanation of existing approaches and a basis for a different learning procedure.

A practical feature is that the method can automatically estimate how much confidence to place in each view. This allows it to accommodate views that are noisy or unreliable, rather than requiring equal trust in every source of information. Experiments with toy and real-world datasets illustrate benefits of the approach, linking the model’s treatment of view reliability to observed learning behavior.
neurips-2007-bayesian-co-training-24b5cd.tldr: A Bayesian account of co-training leads to a convex Gaussian process method that automatically adjusts trust in different data views.

paragraphs: SoftBoost is a boosting algorithm for binary classification when convex combinations of the available base hypotheses may not perfectly separate the training examples. It seeks a large soft margin, allowing the learning objective to accommodate this lack of separability. The method builds its final predictor as a convex combination of hypotheses.

Its robustness mechanism caps the distributions placed over examples, limiting how much weight can concentrate on individual cases. Distribution updates minimize relative entropy subject to these caps and constraints involving the obtained hypotheses. The authors show that the caps correspond to a soft margin in the dual optimization problem and prove a margin within δ of the maximum.

The iteration bound grows logarithmically with the number of examples and inversely with δ squared. The paper identifies cases where LPBoost instead requires iterations growing linearly with the example count. Simulations find SoftBoost about as fast as LPBoost, faster than BrownBoost, and much faster than SmoothBoost; benchmark comparisons also show competitiveness. These empirical comparisons complement the distinct worst-case iteration result.
neurips-2007-boosting-algorithms-for-max.tldr: SoftBoost caps example weights to achieve a provably near-maximal soft margin, with logarithmic iteration dependence on the number of examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a modest ranking capability can be amplified into a very strong one. The performance measure is area under the ROC curve, or AUC. Random guessing can achieve an AUC of one half, so the starting requirement is a weak ranker that performs slightly better than that reference level.

The authors show that such a weak ranker can be efficiently boosted to obtain an AUC arbitrarily close to one. The result concerns approaching that value as closely as desired, rather than asserting that the method must attain it exactly. Its significance is that even a small advantage over random ranking can support a much stronger ranking procedure through boosting.

The paper also extends the result to independent misclassification noise. This extension requires access to a weak ranker that tolerates that noise; noise tolerance is part of the condition for the result. Together, the findings establish an amplification principle for ranking quality, including a noisy-label setting where the required underlying learning capability remains available.
neurips-2007-boosting-the-area-under-the.tldr: A weak ranker with AUC above one half can be efficiently boosted toward AUC one, including under specified noise-tolerance conditions.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces labeling effort by choosing which unlabeled examples should receive labels next. Selecting one example and retraining at every step cannot fully use a labeler capable of handling several examples in parallel. This paper addresses that setting by choosing a batch of examples together at each iteration.

The authors formulate batch selection as continuous optimization over auxiliary variables that represent instance selection. The objective targets the discriminative performance of the classifier while also incorporating unlabeled data. This gives the selection process an explicit classification objective, rather than relying only on heuristic scores for deciding which examples appear informative.

The objective is nonconvex, and the authors adapt a quasi-Newton method to obtain a good local solution. That qualification matters: the optimization procedure is not presented as guaranteeing a global optimum. Empirical studies on UCI datasets find the approach more effective than the contemporary batch active learning methods compared. The results support optimizing batches jointly when labeling can occur in parallel.
neurips-2007-discriminative-batch-mode-a.tldr: The method selects batches for labeling through a classification-focused optimization, with favorable empirical results despite a nonconvex objective.

paragraphs: Speech classification often concerns properties of an entire segment, such as its language, speaker, dialect, or topic. One approach converts speech into tokens and searches for sequences that distinguish those properties. This paper addresses the case where useful keywords are not already known and must instead be constructed automatically from shorter speech units.

The authors formulate keyword construction as feature selection over n-grams of phones: candidate features are sequences of these short units. Their support vector machine approach alternates filter and wrapper stages while building progressively longer keywords. This ties the search for useful sequences to the classification task for which the keywords will be used.

The method is applied to language recognition. The authors report meaningful qualitative and quantitative results, supporting automatic construction of discriminative speech sequences in that application. The contribution is therefore a procedure for developing the vocabulary of a classifier, not merely choosing among a fixed list of predefined words. It offers a way to discover longer useful patterns from shorter available units.
neurips-2007-discriminative-keyword-sele.tldr: An SVM-based feature-selection procedure builds progressively longer phone sequences into useful keywords for speech classification.

paragraphs: Transductive support vector machines face a combinatorial optimization problem whose computational complexity grows exponentially with the number of unlabeled examples. Existing approaches discussed in the paper encounter either high computational cost or solutions trapped at local optima. The authors seek a formulation that makes this difficult optimization more manageable.

Their approach replaces the NP-hard problem with a convex relaxation expressed as a semidefinite program. The central efficiency improvement concerns the size of that relaxed formulation. Relative to another semidefinite relaxation, the proposed method reduces the number of free parameters from O(n²) to O(n), where n is the number of examples.

This reduction means the number of adjustable quantities grows linearly rather than quadratically with the example count. It does not itself state that the entire solver runs in linear time. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show promising performance compared with other leading transductive SVM implementations. The contribution combines a more compact convex formulation with empirical evidence that the relaxation remains useful for learning.
neurips-2007-efficient-convex-relaxation.tldr: A compact semidefinite relaxation makes transductive SVM optimization more efficient by reducing its free parameters from quadratic to linear in dataset size.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Gaussian process framework for random variables associated with network edges. Placing the modeled quantities on edges makes relationships themselves the objects of prediction. The authors construct covariance functions for directed, undirected, and bipartite graphs, allowing the framework to address several different forms of network organization.

A covariance function specifies how the modeled edge variables relate within the Gaussian process prior. Through this formulation, the authors identify a close connection between link prediction and transfer learning, two areas usually treated separately. The framework therefore offers a shared statistical perspective on predicting relationships and using information across related learning problems.

Straightforward Gaussian process inference would be computationally expensive in this setting. The paper develops an efficient learning algorithm capable of handling many observations, making the edge-based formulation more practical. Experiments on several real-world datasets report superior learning capacity. These results provide empirical support for the approach while the covariance constructions supply its broader modeling contribution across different graph types.
neurips-2007-gaussian-process-models-for.tldr: Gaussian processes defined over network edges connect link prediction with transfer learning and support efficient learning from many observations.

paragraphs: The paper presents a compact, low-power hardware network that learns to classify patterns represented by mean neural firing rates. Learning occurs online and in real time, making adaptation part of the network’s operation. The implementation uses integrate-and-fire neurons connected through synapses with two stable weight states.

Synaptic changes follow a local mechanism driven by spikes. During training, a teacher supplies additional input to the output neurons to indicate the desired response. Weights change only when the current produced by the plastic synapses fails to match that desired output. This error-dependent update resembles the perceptron learning rule within a spiking hardware implementation.

Experiments demonstrate robust classification of uncorrelated, linearly separable spatial patterns of mean firing rates. Those properties describe the demonstrated class of patterns and should remain attached to the result. The contribution is a working hardware learning scheme that combines local synaptic adaptation, teacher supervision, and real-time operation, with experimental evidence for the specified classification setting.
neurips-2007-learning-to-classify-comple.tldr: A compact spiking-neuron chip learns online through local, teacher-guided synaptic updates and robustly classifies the tested linearly separable patterns.

paragraphs: The paper studies kernels intended to remain unchanged under translation, rotation, and changes of scale. Its central theoretical finding is that no nontrivial positive definite kernel can be both radial and dilation invariant. This rules out that particular combination of properties within the ordinary positive definite kernel class.

The authors consequently investigate conditionally positive definite kernels, which provide a different mathematical setting for the desired invariance. They develop new analysis, including an elementary derivation of a representer theorem for this class. They also give a support vector machine algorithm that can work with arbitrary conditionally positive definite kernels, connecting the theory to a usable classification method.

With the thin-plate kernel, the classifier needs only one parameter: the amount of regularization. The authors demonstrate effectiveness comparable to an SVM using a Gaussian kernel, which also requires a length-scale parameter. The practical finding is that this kernel choice can reduce the number of parameters while retaining comparable demonstrated classification effectiveness, alongside the paper’s precise restriction on ordinary positive definite kernels.
neurips-2007-learning-with-transformatio.tldr: Conditionally positive definite kernels enable an invariant-kernel SVM approach whose thin-plate version achieves demonstrated Gaussian-SVM effectiveness with one fewer parameter.

paragraphs: Managing server power is useful only when application performance is also considered. This paper applies reinforcement learning to manage both objectives online. The authors test the approach on a laboratory Blade cluster running commercial web application middleware under a changing HTTP workload, giving the controller a realistic setting with varying demand.

A CPU frequency controller is embedded in the servers’ firmware. Its policies are trained using a reward signal that depends on both application performance and CPU power consumption. This makes the learning objective explicitly responsive to the tradeoff the system is meant to manage, rather than judging the controller on power use alone.

The implementation encounters practical difficulties involving different reward functions, limited decision sampling rates, and problems caused by using multiple sensor readings as state variables. The authors describe solutions and demonstrate clear improvements over hand-designed policies and straightforward reinforcement learning implementations. The findings show the importance of adapting the learning setup to operational constraints when applying reinforcement learning to joint performance and power management.
neurips-2007-managing-power-consumption-.tldr: A reinforcement learning CPU controller jointly manages power and application performance, outperforming hand-designed and straightforward RL policies in a laboratory server cluster.

paragraphs: Stochastic event synchrony measures relationships between two time series by aligning their events. It describes timing delay, timing variability, the fraction of spurious events, and average event similarity. This provides a description of how events correspond, allowing the measure to distinguish several aspects of synchrony instead of expressing their relationship through a single timing quantity.

The paper focuses on events in the time-frequency plane. There, event similarity is represented by average frequency offset and frequency variability, producing five parameters overall. These describe synchronization between oscillatory events and offer an alternative to measures based on amplitude or phase. The framework also permits more general one-dimensional and multidimensional point processes.

The authors formulate event alignment as statistical inference on a graphical model and solve it with max-product message passing. They then estimate the synchrony parameters from the alignment using maximum a posteriori estimation. In an application to EEG abnormalities associated with mild cognitive impairment, the reported results indicate significantly improved detection sensitivity. This is evidence from the studied application rather than a universal diagnostic guarantee.
neurips-2007-measuring-neural-synchrony-.tldr: Stochastic event synchrony uses graphical-model alignment to characterize neural events and shows improved EEG sensitivity for detecting mild cognitive impairment.

paragraphs: The maximum-weight independent set problem selects graph vertices with the greatest total weight while excluding pairs connected by an edge. This paper investigates message-passing methods for that task. For ordinary loopy max-product belief propagation, the authors relate estimate quality, conditional on convergence, to how tightly a linear programming relaxation represents the original problem.

That relationship yields sufficient conditions for correctness. The authors then modify max-product so it converges to an optimal solution of a dual optimization problem, and develop a separate iterative procedure to recover an independent-set estimate. Used together, the two procedures give the correct answer when the graph is bipartite and its maximum-weight independent set is unique.

The paper also shows that maximum a posteriori estimation for any probability distribution over finite domains can be reduced to a maximum-weight independent set problem. This gives the graph problem relevance beyond graph selection itself. The authors suggest the reduction could lead to new inference insights and algorithms; it does not extend the stated conditional correctness guarantees to every such inference problem.
neurips-2007-message-passing-for-max-wei.tldr: The paper links message-passing accuracy to optimization relaxations and gives a two-stage method guaranteed correct for bipartite graphs with a unique optimum.

paragraphs: Pairwise maximum entropy models help study how much the relationships between pairs of binary variables explain collective behavior. Their poor scalability makes that analysis difficult in high dimensions, which are common in sensory coding. This paper introduces a near-maximum entropy approach intended to make such investigations feasible for much larger collections of variables.

The NearMaxEnt model has parameters available in closed form and supports easy sampling. These properties allow predictions associated with pairwise maximum entropy modeling to be examined in measurements involving more than a thousand units. The approach therefore expands analysis beyond small subsets whose full joint distributions can still be estimated.

The authors demonstrate the method on natural images whose pixel intensities have been converted into binary values. Pairwise correlations explain the lower-dimensional marginal statistics surprisingly well, but higher-dimensional measurements reveal additional structure that those correlations do not predict. The finding shows why success on small subsets can leave important collective structure undetected, motivating direct examination of larger groups of variables.
neurips-2007-near-maximum-entropy-models.tldr: A scalable near-maximum entropy model reveals high-dimensional image structure that pairwise correlations miss despite explaining smaller subsets well.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering must often learn from a large collection of ratings in which many entries are missing and some users contribute very little. This paper presents Probabilistic Matrix Factorization, or PMF, with computational scaling linear in the number of observed ratings. It reports strong performance on the large, sparse, and highly imbalanced Netflix dataset.

The authors extend PMF with an adaptive prior over model parameters, allowing model capacity to be controlled automatically. A constrained version adds the assumption that users who rated similar sets of movies are likely to share preferences. This uses the pattern of which movies were rated as information about users, and considerably improves generalization for users with very few ratings.

The strongest numerical result belongs to a combination of models. Linearly combining predictions from multiple PMF models and Restricted Boltzmann Machine models produces an error rate of 0.8861, nearly seven percent better than Netflix’s own system. That result supports the combined predictor, while the separate PMF contributions address computational scale, automatic capacity control, and sparse user histories.
neurips-2007-probabilistic-matrix-factor.tldr: PMF scales with observed ratings and improves sparse-user predictions, while an ensemble combining PMF and RBMs beats Netflix’s reported system score.

paragraphs: Controlling a system with many continuous variables and nonlinear dynamics can be computationally difficult. Differential Dynamic Programming approaches the task through local trajectories, avoiding direct exposure to the usual curse of dimensionality. Its drawback in the setting described here is that the resulting controllers are local, leaving a need for a broader control strategy.

The paper introduces Receding Horizon Differential Dynamic Programming, an extension that uses a library of local-control trajectories. The authors describe this extension as enabling stable and robust controllers. The library gives the method a collection of local control behavior to work with, connecting the computational appeal of trajectory-based methods to the construction of more capable controllers.

The approach is evaluated on high-dimensional control tasks involving a simulated swimming robot with multiple links. The experiments show effective handling of problems with at least 34 state dimensions and 14 action dimensions. These results support the method’s ability to circumvent dimensionality difficulties in the tested problems, with the demonstration specifically grounded in simulated robot control.
neurips-2007-receding-horizon-differenti.tldr: Receding Horizon DDP builds stable, robust controllers from local trajectory libraries and handles high-dimensional simulated swimming-robot tasks.

paragraphs: Scene segmentation divides an image into meaningful regions and assigns each a class label. This paper develops a conditional random field model that combines local visual features with information aggregated across large image sections or the whole image. The aim is to let broader scene context contribute alongside evidence near each region.

The authors also address the cost of producing fully labeled training images. Their learning method permits many nodes to remain unlabeled by marginalizing over the unknown labels and maximizing the likelihood of the known ones through gradient ascent. Loopy belief propagation approximates the marginal quantities needed for these calculations.

A Bethe free-energy approximation to the log-likelihood is monitored to control the optimization step size. Experiments show that effective models can be learned from fragmentary annotations and that aggregate features significantly improve segmentation. Results are compared with leading methods on three image datasets. The two contributions work on different parts of the problem: richer contextual evidence improves labeling, while partial-label learning makes incomplete annotations usable for training.
neurips-2007-scene-segmentation-with-crf.tldr: A CRF combines local and image-wide context while learning from incomplete annotations, with experiments showing effective training and improved segmentation.

paragraphs: Unsupervised representation learning seeks structure in data that can provide useful inputs for later supervised learning. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm for learning sparse representations. It places that algorithm in the context of methods that reconstruct their inputs while imposing desirable properties on the representation, and methods that reconstruct probabilistically.

The authors compare their approach theoretically and experimentally with a Restricted Boltzmann Machine. They also propose a criterion for comparing and selecting unsupervised learning machines based on the tradeoff between reconstruction error and the information content of the representation. This makes evaluation sensitive to both how well inputs are recovered and what the representation contains.

The method is demonstrated through feature extraction from handwritten numerals and natural image patches. The authors further show that stacking several levels of these machines and training them sequentially can capture high-order dependencies among input variables. The contribution therefore includes a sparse feature-learning algorithm, a way to judge competing representations, and evidence that layered training can represent more complex relationships in data.
neurips-2007-sparse-feature-learning-for.tldr: An efficient sparse representation learner supports layered feature extraction and a comparison criterion balancing reconstruction error against representation information.

paragraphs: Supervised latent Dirichlet allocation, or sLDA, is a statistical model for documents accompanied by response labels. The goal is to fit a model that can predict response values for new documents, while accommodating several kinds of response. This brings document modeling and the prediction task into the same supervised framework.

The authors derive a maximum-likelihood procedure to estimate the model’s parameters. Some posterior expectations required by that procedure are intractable, so the method uses variational approximations to handle them. Approximate inference is therefore part of how the model is fitted, enabling the proposed estimation procedure to address the quantities it needs.

The paper evaluates prediction in two real-world settings: estimating movie ratings from reviews and estimating web page popularity from text descriptions. The reported comparisons illustrate benefits over regularized regression and over fitting unsupervised LDA before a separate regression step. These findings support using the document responses within the topic-modeling framework, rather than relying solely on topics learned without the prediction target.
neurips-2007-supervised-topic-models-58d.tldr: Supervised LDA models labeled documents for response prediction, showing benefits on movie-rating and web-popularity tasks.

paragraphs: This paper addresses support vector machine classification when the supplied kernel matrix is indefinite. Rather than directly minimizing or stabilizing the resulting nonconvex loss, the authors introduce a proxy kernel matrix. Their method finds that matrix and the support vectors together, making the representation used in the loss part of the learning problem.

The formulation has a robust-classification interpretation: the observed indefinite matrix is treated as a noisy version of an underlying positive semidefinite kernel. This perspective explains why the method can adjust the kernel while fitting the classifier. The supplied matrix provides evidence about the kernel instead of being accepted unchanged as its final form.

The resulting optimization remains convex, and the authors use an analytic center cutting plane method to solve relatively large problems efficiently. They compare the technique with other methods on several datasets. The stated contribution is a computationally tractable formulation for classification with indefinite kernels; the abstract reports comparisons without claiming a particular performance advantage over the alternatives.
neurips-2007-support-vector-machine-clas.tldr: Jointly learning support vectors and a proxy kernel turns classification with an indefinite kernel into a convex robust-learning formulation.

paragraphs: Planning with partial observability involves beliefs about the state, and those belief spaces can be high-dimensional. Yet point-based POMDP algorithms often approximate good solutions successfully. This paper investigates why, focusing on a covering number: a measure of how many points are needed to represent the relevant belief space at the required resolution.

The authors show that an approximately optimal solution can be computed in time polynomial in the covering number of the space reachable from a given initial belief. A small covering number only for beliefs reachable under an optimal policy is a weaker condition, and planning remains NP-hard under that condition. The distinction concerns which reachable space is small.

However, if a suitable set of points covering the optimal reachable space is supplied, an approximate solution can be computed in polynomial time. This separates a useful compact representation from the difficulty of obtaining it. The analysis also highlights helpful structures, including fully observed variables, sparsely supported or smooth beliefs, and circulant transition matrices, offering explanations for practical approximation success.
neurips-2007-what-makes-some-pomdp-probl.tldr: POMDP approximation depends on how compactly reachable beliefs can be covered, with a crucial distinction between all reachable beliefs and those under an optimal policy.
